claims.text: Conventional high-thermal-load processing of AlCrFeNiSi powder produces non-uniform microstructures, residual stresses, and inferior mechanical properties.

A two-step route comprising vacuum debinding followed by controlled solid-state sintering can overcome the residual stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Vacuum debinding reduces oxidation during binder removal.
Vacuum debinding reduces thermal gradients during binder removal.
Reduced oxygen uptake and thermal gradients decrease oxidation at powder interfaces and local stress concentrations.
Solid-state sintering just below the alloy melting point promotes uniform densification without creating large thermal gradients.
Controlled solid-state sintering permits gradual densification and grain growth without excessive thermal history.
The proposed route produces a more homogeneous microstructure with improved grain-boundary integrity.
The proposed route minimizes residual stress in the consolidated component.
Relative to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing, the proposed route will produce AlCrFeNiSi components with lower residual thermal stresses.
Relative to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing, the proposed route will produce more uniform and finer microstructural features.
Relative to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing, the proposed route will improve tensile strength and toughness.
Laser-melting additive-manufacturing routes involve rapid solidification and high residual thermal stresses.
Laser-melting additive-manufacturing routes degrade the mechanical properties of the resulting components.
The proposed processing route is applicable to miniature AlCrFeNiSi components with characteristic dimensions from sub-millimeter to a few millimeters.
Applicability depends on component thermal mass and sintering kinetics permitting consolidation below the alloy melting point.
Results may not transfer directly to bulk components or alloy systems with substantially different sintering behavior.
Residual-stress diffraction measurements, microscopy, mechanical testing, and oxidation-state analysis can distinguish the proposed route from a conventional high-thermal-load control.
